subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the human lungs, gas exchange takes place mainly in the:
questions.explain: The alveoli are the tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

questions.q: Why does the wall of an alveolus being only one cell thick help gas exchange?
options: It provides a short diffusion distance for gases
It increases the volume of air held
It slows down the movement of gases
questions.explain: A thin, one-cell-thick wall gives a short diffusion pathway, allowing gases to diffuse quickly.

questions.q: The large number of alveoli in the lungs is important because it:
options: Provides a large surface area for diffusion
Prevents carbon dioxide from leaving the blood
questions.explain: Many alveoli give a very large total surface area, increasing the rate of gas exchange.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of oxygen is present in inspired (breathed-in) air?
questions.explain: Inspired air contains roughly 21% oxygen, while expired air contains about 16%.

questions.q: Compared with inspired air, expired (breathed-out) air contains:
options: More oxygen and less carbon dioxide
Less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
Less carbon dioxide and less water vapour
questions.explain: Respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, so expired air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which cells in the lining of the airways secrete mucus?
questions.explain: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps dust and pathogens in the airways.

questions.q: What is the role of the cilia lining the airways?
options: To secrete mucus onto the airway surface
To absorb oxygen into the blood
To sweep mucus and trapped particles towards the throat
questions.explain: Cilia beat to move trapped mucus and particles up and out of the airways, protecting the lungs.

questions.q: During vigorous exercise, a student's breathing rate increases. This mainly allows the body to:
options: Remove excess lactic acid through the lungs
Supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide
Reduce the amount of water lost from the lungs
Increase the nitrogen taken into the blood
questions.explain: Faster breathing increases oxygen supply for respiration and speeds removal of the extra carbon dioxide produced.

questions.q: Which structures work together to bring about breathing (ventilation) in humans?
options: The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles
The heart and the pulmonary artery
The cilia and the goblet cells
questions.explain: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles change the volume of the thorax to move air in and out.

questions.q: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
options: Relaxes and moves upward into a dome shape
Contracts and flattens, increasing thorax volume
Contracts and pushes air out of the lungs
Stays still while the ribs move down
questions.explain: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing thoracic volume and lowering pressure so air moves in.

questions.q: Aerobic respiration is best described as the chemical reactions in cells that:
options: Break down glucose without using oxygen
Use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy
Build up glucose using light energy
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down nutrients such as glucose, releasing energy for the cell.

questions.q: Which word equation correctly represents aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration converts glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.

questions.q: Which balanced symbol equation represents aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: The balanced equation is C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O, with six oxygen, carbon dioxide and water molecules.

questions.q: The waste products released by aerobic respiration in a human muscle cell are:
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water as waste products.

questions.q: A student breathes out through a tube into limewater and the limewater turns milky (cloudy). This shows that expired air contains:
options: A high level of carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Limewater turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide, which is produced by respiration.

questions.q: During hard exercise, anaerobic respiration in human muscles produces:
questions.explain: In human muscles, anaerobic respiration breaks glucose down into lactic acid.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces:
questions.explain: In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Compared with aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration releases:
options: More energy from each glucose molecule
Less energy from each glucose molecule
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule because glucose is only partly broken down.

questions.q: In bread-making, yeast is mixed into dough and the dough rises. Which product of anaerobic respiration in yeast causes the dough to rise?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide produced by yeast forms bubbles in the dough, making it rise.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration is best defined as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules to release energy:
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration releases energy from nutrient molecules without using oxygen.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610) syllabus; Gas Exchange & Respiration
